_about: PRO batch 42: era 4, The Veteran (34-37), set 2.

scenarios.title: The Analytics Report
scenarios.text: The club's analysts present a chart in a meeting room with the lights down: your leg speed, season by season, sloping gently downhill. Your leg, the chart says, is getting older faster than you are.

choices.label: Ask what the chart can't see
choices.result: What can't the chart see? You ask calmly, and the room goes quiet. The analysts admit they don't measure accuracy under pressure, and they add a column.

choices.label: Train against the chart
choices.result: A copy of the chart goes on your garage wall. Every morning that summer is an argument with it, and by camp the slope has flattened.

choices.label: Laugh it off at dinner
choices.result: The chart, described at dinner in your most dramatic voice. Your family laughs until they cry, and it stops feeling like a verdict.

scenarios.title: Losing a Step
scenarios.text: Your longest kick in practice is five yards shorter than last year's. Nobody has said anything, but the coaches have started setting up the long drills when you're in the training room.

choices.label: Rebuild your approach
choices.result: A longer approach, a new step, six weeks of work. The five yards come back as three, and you take the three gratefully.

choices.label: Talk to {coach} first
choices.result: The question, asked before anyone else does: what does the club need from you now? {coach} is honest: accuracy inside fifty, and a steady head.

choices.label: Make peace with it
choices.result: Five yards, accepted. You become the most accurate kicker inside forty-five in the league, and nobody asks about the long ones for a while.

scenarios.title: The Owner's Funeral
scenarios.text: The owner of the club that first signed you has died at eighty-one. His family asks if you'll speak at the memorial, because he used to talk about you at dinner.

choices.label: Speak about the man
choices.result: Not the owner, the man: the way he knew the equipment staff's kids' names. His widow holds your hand afterward for a long time.

choices.label: Tell one story about him
choices.result: One story, the one about your rookie contract and the handwritten note he slipped into it. The room laughs and then goes very quiet.

choices.label: Write to the family instead
choices.result: A letter to the family, long and personal, because you're no good at podiums. They read it at the reception, and his grandson keeps it.

scenarios.title: A Midnight Call From an Old Teammate
scenarios.text: A teammate from your rookie year calls at midnight. He's broke, the house is gone, and he doesn't know who else to call. He apologizes four times before he says why.

choices.label: Help him get back up
choices.result: A plan, not a check: an advisor you trust, a job interview with a friend, a loan for the first three months. He's on his feet by summer.

choices.label: Send what he needs tonight
choices.result: The money he needs, sent before you hang up. He cries on the phone, and you don't ask when he'll pay it back.

choices.label: Listen, and point him to help
choices.result: An hour of listening, and the number for the union's assistance program. It's the right help, and you wonder afterward if it was enough.

scenarios.title: The Retired Players' Meeting
scenarios.text: Retired players are organizing for better health care, and they want a current player at the meeting. As your team's union rep, it's you. The room is full of men who limp.

choices.label: Speak for them
choices.result: A short speech about the players who built the league you play in. A man with two canes shakes your hand and won't let go.

choices.label: Bring it to the current players
choices.result: Their stories, carried back to your locker room. Forty current players sign the petition by Friday, and the retired players notice.

choices.label: Learn the details
choices.result: The health care proposal, studied line by line until you can explain it to anyone. It's dry and important, and you become the person people ask.

scenarios.title: The Old Lineman's Memory
scenarios.text: At a team reunion, a lineman you played beside for years looks at you kindly and doesn't remember your name. His wife squeezes his arm and says it quietly for him.

choices.label: Sit with him all evening
choices.result: The whole evening, beside him, telling him stories he used to tell. Some of them he remembers, and he laughs in the right places.

choices.label: Talk to his wife
choices.result: His wife, in the hallway, tells you everything: the hits, the doctors, the bad days. You leave with her number and a promise to visit.

choices.label: Call the union about it
choices.result: The union, called the next morning about the retired players' care program. It's a small thing to do, and you do it twice more that month.

scenarios.title: The Last of Your Draft Class
scenarios.text: You're the last player from your draft class still in the league. The other two hundred and fifty-five are coaches, salesmen, broadcasters, or nobody knows. A reporter wants a quote.

choices.label: Call a few of them
choices.result: A few old draft-class numbers, called one evening. Two of them pick up, and you talk for hours about the week you were all twenty-two.

choices.label: Give the reporter something true
choices.result: Lucky, you tell the reporter, and stubborn, and well looked after. The quote runs, and three old teammates text you that it was exactly right.

choices.label: Don't make a thing of it
choices.result: No quote, no fuss. You go to practice, kick, go home. Being the last one feels like something you shouldn't jinx.

scenarios.title: The Kid Who Was Born on Draft Day
scenarios.text: A rookie mentions at lunch, cheerfully, that he was born the week you were drafted. The table goes silent, and then the whole specialists' room starts laughing.

choices.label: Laugh harder than anyone
choices.result: The hardest laugh at the table is yours. By dinner the rookie has a new nickname for you, and you secretly love it.

choices.label: Tell him about that week
choices.result: The week you were drafted, told in full: the motel, the phone call, {parent}'s face. The rookie listens like it's history, which it is.

choices.label: Take it as a challenge
choices.result: A challenge, quietly accepted: you'll still be here when he's a veteran. You kick an extra fifty that afternoon, smiling the whole time.

scenarios.title: The Short-Term Contract
scenarios.text: Your agent calls with the spring's news: no club is willing to offer more than a year or two. 'They love you,' your agent says. 'They just don't love your birthday.'

choices.label: Take the best two-year deal
choices.result: Two years, the best of the offers, signed in a week. It's less than you hoped and more than some expected, and the uncertainty stops.

choices.label: Bet on a one-year deal
choices.result: One year, and you bet on yourself to earn the next. Every practice is an audition again, and you feel twenty-two in the worst and best ways.

choices.label: Ask your family what they want
choices.result: The offers, laid out at the kitchen table for everyone. The kids vote for the club closest to their grandparents, and that settles it.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Discount
scenarios.text: The club asks you to take less to stay, a lot less, because 'you're family here'. The general manager says it twice and puts a hand on your shoulder the second time.

choices.label: Take the discount
choices.result: The discount, accepted, because you want to finish here. The locker room notices, and so does the front office, and it feels right most days.

choices.label: Counter with a fair number
choices.result: A counter, fair and calm, through your agent. They meet you two-thirds of the way, and you sign without hard feelings.

choices.label: Look elsewhere
choices.result: Elsewhere, then. You thank them sincerely and start packing your locker in your head, and two clubs call by the end of the week.

scenarios.title: The Release Rumors
scenarios.text: The papers say you could be cut before the season starts. A radio host has started a countdown. Your neighbor asks, kindly, over the fence, if you're okay.

choices.label: Make the decision hard for them
choices.result: Every practice, the best of your summer. If they cut you, they'll have to explain it, and by the last preseason game nobody's talking about it.

choices.label: Ask {coach} directly
choices.result: {coach}, asked plainly in the parking lot. The answer is honest: it's close. Knowing helps more than the rumors did.

choices.label: Prepare the family
choices.result: The family, prepared over dinner for either outcome. Nobody panics, and the kids make a list of cities they'd like.

scenarios.title: The Free Agent Market
scenarios.text: Your first week at a new club, after a spring with far fewer calls than you expected. The locker has a nameplate with your name spelled slightly wrong.

choices.label: Fix the nameplate yourself
choices.result: A marker, a steady hand, and the nameplate fixed before practice. The equipment manager laughs and makes you a new one by lunch.

choices.label: Prove the spring wrong
choices.result: Every rep that week, sharp and clean. The clubs that didn't call will see the film, and you want them to wince.

choices.label: Learn every name by Friday
choices.result: Every name in the building, learned by Friday, from the head coach to the laundry staff. It's the fastest you've ever felt at home.

scenarios.title: The Backup Role
scenarios.text: A club offers you a job: backup kicker, behind a twenty-four-year-old with a huge leg. The money is fine. It's the job young kickers hold while they wait their turn, and you are not young.

choices.label: Take it and teach
choices.result: The job, taken, and the young kicker gets everything you know. He's better by midseason, and the room calls you 'coach' half seriously.

choices.label: Take it and compete
choices.result: The job, taken, and you compete for the real one every day. The young kicker gets better because of you, whether he likes it or not.

choices.label: Turn it down
choices.result: No, politely. You'd rather start somewhere small than sit somewhere big, and your agent sighs and makes three more calls.
